fallbackText: A healthy child playing in a playground suddenly collapses. A nurse approaches.

options.text: Emergency care provided to infants and children experiencing respiratory or cardiac arrest
Management provided when a baby is not crying after birth

feedback.text: PBLS is the emergency care given to infants and children in respiratory or cardiac arrest, until advanced help arrives.

feedback.text: Unresponsiveness is the trigger for PBLS. Sleep, normal play and an ongoing seizure with breathing intact do not call for life support.

title: Emergencies requiring PBLS
objective: Recognize situations requiring Pediatric Basic Life Support
prompt: Drag each condition into the correct box.

feedback.text: Drowning, choking, cardiac arrest and severe trauma can all progress to arrest. A cold or a mild fever does not call for life support.

title: Pediatric age group
objective: Classify children into the appropriate PBLS age groups
prompt: Which age group is covered under PBLS?

options.text: Infants from 28 days of age and children until puberty; newborns 28 days and under are covered by NRP or neonatal life support

feedback.text: PBLS covers infants from 28 days until the onset of puberty. Newborns in the first 28 days fall under neonatal resuscitation, and beyond puberty adult BLS applies.

options.text: Infant: five back slaps then five chest thrusts, alternating. Child: five back blows first then five abdominal thrusts, alternating
Infant: abdominal thrusts. Child: back slaps

feedback.text: Infants receive five back slaps then five chest thrusts, since abdominal thrusts are contraindicated. Conscious children aged 1 year and above receive five back blows first, then five abdominal thrusts.

title: Establishing a team leader
objective: Demonstrate appropriate leadership behaviours
scenario: A 5-year-old is in cardiac arrest. Four nurses arrive and everyone talks simultaneously with no direction.
prompt: What is the MOST important immediate action?
fallbackText: Four nurses arrive at a 5-year-old in cardiac arrest. Everyone is talking at once and nobody is directing the resuscitation.

feedback.text: An effective resuscitation team requires one clearly identified leader who directs all actions.

title: Responding to an instruction
objective: Apply closed-loop communication during CPR
scenario: The leader says, apply the AED. The nurse remains silent and does nothing.
prompt: Which communication style is BEST?
fallbackText: The team leader instructs a nurse to apply the AED. The nurse stays silent and does not move.

options.text: Say applying AED now, then confirm on completion

feedback.text: Closed-loop communication means receive the order, acknowledge it, then confirm completion. This confirms instructions are heard and acted upon.

title: Identify the communication pattern
objective: Apply closed-loop communication during CPR
scenario: The leader says, Sarah, switch compressors. Sarah replies, switching compressors. After changing positions Sarah says, compressor changed.
prompt: This is an example of:
fallbackText: The leader asks Sarah to switch compressors. Sarah confirms she is switching, and confirms again once the change is complete.

feedback.text: The instruction is acknowledged on receipt and confirmed on completion. That closed loop is what tells the leader the task is actually done.

title: The compressor is tiring
objective: Assign roles and responsibilities effectively
scenario: The compressor appears exhausted and compression depth is decreasing.
prompt: What should the team leader do?

feedback.text: Compressor fatigue reduces CPR quality. Rotate roughly every two minutes proactively, and switch immediately if quality deteriorates.

title: Full resuscitation
objective: Identify the principles of effective team dynamics during paediatric resuscitation
scenario: The leader assigns a role, Maria acknowledges, the AED is applied, Maria says AED ready, the leader says everyone clear, a shock is delivered, and the leader says resume CPR.
prompt: Which team dynamic principles are demonstrated?
fallbackText: During CPR the leader names Maria and assigns her the AED. Maria acknowledges, applies it, and reports it ready. The leader calls everyone clear, a shock is delivered, and the leader directs the team to resume CPR.

options.text: Leadership, role assignment and closed-loop communication

feedback.text: The leader directs, names a specific person for a specific task, and receives confirmation at each step. All three principles are present together.

title: Situational awareness
objective: Demonstrate situational awareness during resuscitation
scenario: During CPR, a rescuer notices that rescue breaths are causing visible gastric distension but says nothing.
prompt: What should this rescuer do?

options.text: Continue without comment, since it is not their role
Speak up immediately: I can see gastric distension, suggest reducing breath volume
Wait until the team leader asks

feedback.text: Situational awareness and assertive communication together mean every team member has a responsibility to speak up when they identify a safety concern. This is a core principle of effective resuscitation team dynamics.

title: Role assignment
objective: Assign roles and responsibilities effectively
prompt: When assigning roles during resuscitation, what is the recommended approach?

options.text: Assign roles after CPR has started
Use first names and specify roles clearly, for example Maria you are on compressions, Priya manage the airway
Assign only one role, the compressor

feedback.text: Clear, name-specific role assignment prevents duplication and gaps. Each member must know exactly what they are responsible for.

title: Post-resuscitation debriefing
objective: Identify the principles of effective team dynamics during paediatric resuscitation
scenario: The resuscitation team successfully achieves return of spontaneous circulation. The team leader calls the team together.
prompt: What is the PURPOSE of a post-resuscitation debrief?

options.text: To document the case for legal purposes only
To identify what went well and what can be improved to optimise future performance
Debriefs are optional and rarely useful

feedback.text: Structured debriefing after resuscitation improves team performance, reduces errors in subsequent events and supports team wellbeing. It is a standard component of quality resuscitation programmes.
